Purpose is to provide an inkjet recording method for forming high-quality color image on a thick recording medium having low thermal conductance rate. The present invention is a single-pass inkjet recording method using an ink set including at least two active ray-curing color inks, and a recording medium having thermal conductivity of less than 0.10 W/(m·K) and thickness of 0.4 mm or more. The ink set containing two color inks satisfy only condition (a), and the ink set containing three or more color inks satisfy conditions (a) and (b): (a) most downstream color ink has a gelation temperature which is 3.0° C. to 15.0° C. higher than that of most upstream color ink, and (b) second or subsequent color ink from the most upstream position in conveyance direction has a gelation temperature which is the same as or higher than that of an adjacent color ink at the upstream position.

The invention provides an inkjet recording method capable of forming high-quality color images on thick recording media having low thermal conductivity. In particular, the method is suitable for recording on media that are difficult to heat or cool uniformly, such as thick paper, boards, panels, or other substrates with insulating properties.

The inkjet recording method is performed as a single-pass inkjet process. In this process, a recording medium is conveyed in one direction, and a plurality of inkjet heads discharge inks onto the medium in sequence during a single pass. The ink set used in the method contains at least two active ray-curing color inks. These inks are cured by irradiation with active rays, such as ultraviolet rays or electron beams, after being applied to the recording medium.

The recording medium used in the method has a thermal conductivity of less than 0.10 W/(m·K) and a thickness of 0.4 mm or more. Because such a medium has low thermal conductivity and relatively large thickness, heat transfer within the medium is limited. As a result, temperature control of the ink after landing can be difficult, and image defects such as color mixing, uneven gloss, or reduced sharpness may occur if the ink properties are not properly controlled.

To address this issue, the method controls the gelation temperatures of the color inks according to their order of application. When the ink set contains two color inks, the color ink discharged from the most downstream inkjet head has a gelation temperature that is higher than the gelation temperature of the color ink discharged from the most upstream inkjet head. The difference between these gelation temperatures is set within a range of 3.0°C to 15.0°C. By establishing this temperature difference, the inks can gel appropriately after landing, thereby suppressing excessive spreading and inter-color bleeding while maintaining good image quality.

When the ink set contains three or more color inks, the gelation temperature of each color ink is controlled relative to the ink discharged immediately before it. Specifically, each subsequent color ink, in the downstream direction, has a gelation temperature equal to or higher than that of the adjacent upstream color ink. In addition, the gelation temperature of the most downstream color ink satisfies the same condition described above: it is 3.0°C to 15.0°C higher than the gelation temperature of the most upstream color ink.

Through this configuration, the single-pass inkjet recording method can stably form high-quality color images even on thick, low-thermal-conductivity recording media. The controlled relationship among the gelation temperatures of the inks helps regulate ink behavior on the medium, improving image sharpness, reducing bleeding between colors, and enabling reliable curing of the final printed image.
outputs.L4:
A single-pass inkjet recording method is provided for forming high-quality color images on recording media that are difficult to process by ordinary inkjet techniques, particularly thick recording media having relatively low thermal conductivity. The method uses an active ray-curing color ink set, such as an ultraviolet-curable ink set, in which each ink contains a colorant and an active ray-curable component and is capable of undergoing temperature-dependent gelation. The inks are ejected onto the recording medium from a plurality of inkjet heads arranged in the transport direction of the medium, and the deposited inks are then cured by irradiation with active rays.

In this recording method, the gelation temperatures of the respective color inks are controlled according to the order in which the inks are applied. Specifically, an ink positioned downstream in the transport direction is set to have a gelation temperature equal to or higher than that of an ink positioned upstream. In a preferred configuration, the gelation temperature of the most downstream ink is higher than the gelation temperature of the most upstream ink by 3.0°C to 15.0°C. By establishing this relationship among the gelation temperatures, the inks deposited later can appropriately maintain or control their viscosity after landing on the recording medium, even when the medium is thick and heat is not readily transferred through it.

This temperature design suppresses excessive spreading, bleeding, and mixing of adjacent color inks, while also promoting smooth dot formation and stable overlap of different ink colors. As a result, image defects such as color unevenness, graininess, mottling, and reduced sharpness can be minimized. The method is particularly effective in single-pass recording, where high-speed printing is performed without repeatedly scanning the same region and where control of ink behavior immediately after landing is especially important.

Accordingly, the proposed method enables stable formation of high-density, high-definition color images on thick recording media, including media that have low thermal conductivity and are therefore prone to insufficient temperature control during printing. By using an active ray-curing color ink set with gelation temperatures arranged so that downstream inks are equal to or higher than upstream inks, and preferably with a 3.0°C to 15.0°C difference between the most downstream and most upstream inks, the method improves image quality and expands the range of recording media suitable for high-speed single-pass inkjet printing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the purpose and main claim of this patent abstract about a single-pass inkjet recording method using active ray-curing inks on thick low-thermal-conductivity media.
counterfactuals.output:
The patent abstract describes a **single-pass inkjet recording method** for printing on relatively thick recording media with **low thermal conductivity**, such as boards or similar substrates. The method uses **active ray-curing inks**—inks that cure when exposed to radiation such as ultraviolet light—and addresses problems that can occur when printing and curing these inks on media that do not easily conduct heat.

Its main claim is that high-quality inkjet recording can be achieved by controlling the relationship between the inks’ **surface tension** and the **thickness of the recording medium**. Specifically, the method uses at least two active ray-curing inks, including the first and last inks deposited, and sets their surface tensions so that they differ by a defined amount depending on the medium thickness. This control helps prevent image defects such as bleeding, uneven spreading, or poor curing during high-speed single-pass printing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise patent-style abstract describing an inkjet recording method for high-quality color images on thick recording media with thermal conductivity below 0.10 W/(m·K), specifying gelation temperature conditions for two-color and multi-color ink sets.
counterfactuals.output: An inkjet recording method is provided for forming a high-quality color image on a thick recording medium having a thermal conductivity of less than 0.10 W/(m·K). The method includes ejecting, onto the recording medium, an ink set comprising radiation-curable inks that undergo sol-gel phase transition, each ink being heated to a sol state during discharge and gelled after landing, followed by irradiation to cure the image. For a two-color ink set, the gelation temperatures of the two inks are controlled so that the absolute difference therebetween is not more than 10°C. For an ink set of three or more colors, the gelation temperatures of all inks are controlled within a range of not more than 10°C between the maximum and minimum gelation temperatures. By equalizing gelation behavior on low-thermal-conductivity thick media, color mixing, beading, density unevenness, and dot-size variation are suppressed, thereby enabling stable formation of sharp, high-density color images.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the invention in this patent claim: an ink set of active ray-curing color inks used in single-pass inkjet printing on a medium at least 0.4 mm thick and having low thermal conductivity, including the required gelation temperature relationships.
counterfactuals.output:
The claimed invention is an **ink set for high-speed single-pass inkjet printing** in which each ink is an **active ray-curing color ink**—typically a UV/LED-curable ink—that can be jetted as a liquid, then rapidly immobilized by gelation and finally cured by irradiation.

In plain terms, the invention addresses printing on difficult media such as thick plastic sheets, boards, cards, or similar substrates that are:

- **at least 0.4 mm thick**, and  
- have **low thermal conductivity**, meaning they do not quickly draw heat away from the ink droplets.

Because such media do not cool droplets efficiently, freshly landed ink can remain fluid too long. In single-pass printing, where the substrate moves once under fixed inkjet heads and different colors are deposited in rapid succession, this can cause:

- color-to-color bleeding,
- dot spreading,
- poor image sharpness,
- mottling or uneven density,
- reduced edge definition.

The invention uses **gel-type active ray-curing inks** whose viscosity sharply increases when the ink temperature falls below a certain point, called the **gelation temperature**. After landing, the ink gels or semi-solidifies before final UV curing, thereby holding the dot shape and suppressing inter-color mixing.

The ink set includes multiple color inks, for example cyan, magenta, yellow, black, and possibly other colors. Each ink has a gelation temperature, and the claim requires that these gelation temperatures satisfy specified relationships. The essential idea is:

1. **The ink is heated above its gelation temperature during jetting**, so it is low-viscosity enough to be discharged reliably from the inkjet head.

2. **After landing on the medium, the ink temperature falls below its gelation temperature**, so the droplet gels and becomes immobilized before it can excessively spread or bleed.

3. **The gelation temperatures of the different color inks are controlled relative to one another**, especially according to the order in which the inks are applied in the single-pass printer.

In practical terms, the required relationship is that the inks printed earlier in the single-pass sequence have gelation behavior that allows them to immobilize before later colors land on or near them. Thus, the gelation temperatures are selected so that an earlier-applied color ink gels at least as readily as, or at a higher temperature than, a later-applied ink. This helps the first ink resist disturbance or mixing when the next color is deposited.

So, if the print order is, for example:

> Color ink 1 → Color ink 2 → Color ink 3 → Color ink 4

then the gelation temperatures are arranged so that the upstream or earlier inks have gelation temperatures that are not lower than those of downstream inks, e.g.:

> Gelation temperature of ink 1 ≥ gelation temperature of ink 2 ≥ gelation temperature of ink 3 ≥ gelation temperature of ink 4

or at least the claim requires a defined difference or order between the gelation temperatures of the inks according to their printing order.

The purpose of these gelation-temperature relationships is to make sure that, on a thick low-thermal-conductivity medium, each deposited droplet becomes sufficiently immobilized before the next color is applied, even though the medium itself does not cool the ink quickly.

After the droplets are positioned and gelled, they are exposed to an **active ray**, such as ultraviolet light or electron beam radiation, which polymerizes and hardens the inks into a final cured image.

In short, the invention is an **ink set for single-pass UV-curable inkjet printing on thick, poorly heat-conductive media**, where the individual color inks are designed with coordinated gelation temperatures so that earlier-deposited inks gel quickly enough to prevent bleeding and maintain high image quality before final radiation curing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical summary for a Japanese patent on active ray-curable inkjet inks, where the downstream ink has a higher gelation temperature than the upstream ink and three or more inks must have nondecreasing gelation temperatures along the conveyance direction.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Summary: Japanese Patent — Active Ray-Curable Inkjet Ink Set / Image Forming Method

### Field of the Invention
The patent relates to an **inkjet image forming method** and an **ink set** using **active ray-curable inks**, such as ultraviolet-curable or electron-beam-curable inks. The technology is particularly directed to **multi-color inkjet printing** in which multiple inks are discharged sequentially onto a recording medium while the medium is conveyed in a predetermined direction.

### Technical Problem
In active ray-curable inkjet printing, inks may be designed to **gel** at a certain temperature after landing on the recording medium. Gelation helps suppress excessive spreading, coalescence between adjacent droplets, and color mixing before curing.

However, when several inks are printed sequentially, differences in gelation behavior can cause image defects such as:

- bleeding between colors,
- uneven dot shape,
- loss of sharpness,
- gloss nonuniformity,
- poor color reproducibility,
- density unevenness, and
- surface roughness caused by incompatible flow or leveling behavior.

The patent addresses the problem of achieving **high-quality multi-color images** by controlling the relationship between the **gelation temperatures** of inks arranged along the conveyance direction.

### Core Technical Concept
The invention provides an inkjet printing system using **three or more active ray-curable inks**, where the inks are arranged in the order in which they are applied to the recording medium.

A key requirement is that the **gelation temperatures of the inks do not decrease downstream**.

In other words, if the inks are applied in sequence along the conveyance direction:

\[
Ink_1 \rightarrow Ink_2 \rightarrow Ink_3 \rightarrow \cdots
\]

then their gelation temperatures satisfy:

\[
T_{g1} \leq T_{g2} \leq T_{g3} \leq \cdots
\]

where \(T_g\) represents the gelation temperature of each ink.

More specifically, the patent requires that a **downstream ink has a gelation temperature equal to or higher than that of an upstream ink**, and for **three or more inks**, the gelation temperatures are arranged in a **nondecreasing order** along the conveyance direction.

### Meaning of “Upstream” and “Downstream”
- **Upstream ink**: an ink discharged earlier onto the recording medium.
- **Downstream ink**: an ink discharged later, from a printhead located farther along the conveyance path.

The recording medium moves in the conveyance direction, and the printheads are positioned in sequence. The patent controls the gelation temperatures according to this physical printhead order.

### Active Ray-Curable Ink
The inks are curable by exposure to active radiation, typically:

- ultraviolet light,
- electron beams,
- visible active rays, or
- other actinic radiation capable of initiating polymerization.

The inks generally contain:

- a polymerizable compound, such as a monomer or oligomer,
- a photopolymerization initiator, when UV curing is used,
- a colorant,
- a gelling agent or wax-like compound,
- optional dispersants, sensitizers, inhibitors, surfactants, and other additives.

### Gelation Temperature Control
Each ink has a defined gelation temperature. The gelation temperature may be controlled by adjusting:

- type and amount of gelling agent,
- wax or crystalline compound content,
- monomer composition,
- oligomer structure,
- pigment dispersion components,
- molecular weight distribution,
- polarity and compatibility of ink components.

The invention does not merely require gelation in general; it requires a specific **relative ordering** of gelation temperatures among multiple inks.

### Printing Method
A representative method includes:

1. Conveying a recording medium in a predetermined direction.
2. Discharging a first active ray-curable ink from an upstream inkjet head.
3. Discharging second and subsequent active ray-curable inks from downstream inkjet heads.
4. Ensuring that the downstream inks have gelation temperatures equal to or higher than upstream inks.
5. Irradiating the deposited inks with active rays to cure the inks and fix the image.

The curing may be performed:

- after all inks are deposited,
- between selected ink applications,
- or by a combination of pinning exposure and final curing exposure.

### Functional Effect
By arranging the gelation temperatures in a nondecreasing order from upstream to downstream, the system can better control droplet behavior after landing.

The expected technical effects include:

- suppression of inter-color bleeding,
- reduced coalescence of droplets,
- improved dot placement and dot shape,
- enhanced image sharpness,
- stable color reproduction,
- improved gloss uniformity,
- prevention of excessive ink spreading,
- improved layered ink compatibility,
- higher image density and definition,
- better curing uniformity.

The arrangement is especially useful when printing with three or more inks, such as cyan, magenta, yellow, and black, or additional colors such as white, light cyan, light magenta, orange, green, violet, or clear ink.

### Claim-Like Summary
The invention can be summarized as an inkjet image forming method or ink set in which:

- a plurality of active ray-curable inks are used;
- the plurality includes at least three inks;
- the inks are discharged onto a recording medium in sequence along a conveyance direction;
- each ink has a gelation temperature;
- for any upstream and downstream relationship, the downstream ink has a gelation temperature equal to or higher than the upstream ink; and
- the inks are cured by irradiation with active rays.

### Technical Significance
The patent’s key contribution is not simply the use of gel-type UV-curable inkjet inks, but the **systematic ordering of gelation temperatures** across multiple inks according to the printhead sequence. This temperature-ordering rule provides a practical way to stabilize multi-color ink deposition before curing and thereby improve final image quality.
